Diff for QUALITY not exact match: all 5 top-level keys present. THIRD-PASS GUARDS (2026-09-05, same day as the schema restructure): the subtlest failure mode caught yet — chronology silently turned into causation, and 'creates room for a goal' silently turned into 'directly produces the goal.' Case 1's what_i_notice.pattern is the reference case: 'Your evening currently runs from dinner through TV or scrolling until midnight, while you said you want to do creative work in that window' — a chronological/goal-connection statement with NO claim that late-night screens cause tiredness or that the visitor established how rested they feel. Case 1's change_to_try.what_it_may_change is the reference case for room-vs-produce: 'the change creates the opening, it does not fill it' — explicit, not implied. Case 1's what_to_watch_for.signs_it_may_be_helping is the reference case for the 4-step template: (1) direct mechanical effect happens — 'the screen-free window exists' — before (2) visitor uses the room, (3) visitor reaches the stated goal activity, (4) open catch-all — never opening with a presupposed downstream feeling like sleep or energy. Case 1's why_not_start_elsewhere never claims the alternative (moving the phone) 'does nothing to address' anything — it's 'a reasonable experiment' targeting 'a different part of the routine.' input.routine: Wake at 6:30, snooze the alarm twice, check my phone in bed for 20 minutes before getting up, shower, coffee, commute 30 min listening to a podcast, at my desk by 9. Meetings 9-12, lunch at my desk, more meetings 1-4, try to do focused work 4-6 but usually get interrupted. Home by 7, dinner, then TV or scrolling until midnight.
input.goals: Better focus, less exhausted, want to do creative work in the evenings but never have energy
input.painPoints: The 2pm slump is brutal. I feel behind before I even start.

what_i_notice.pattern: Your evening currently runs from dinner through TV or scrolling until midnight, while you said you want to do creative work in that window but never have energy for it. The creative time you want and the time you actually have are the same block — the question is what fills it.
what_i_notice.why_it_matters: You named evening creative work as something you want more of. That window is already there; right now it ends with TV or scrolling rather than the work you described wanting to do.

change_to_try.change: Pick a point in the evening — say, 9pm or wherever feels feasible — and treat it as when screens stop and the creative window opens. Even 30 minutes is enough to start.
change_to_try.why_this_one: Your meetings, commute, and interrupted 4-6pm block are largely outside your control on any given day. The evening is not. This is a small boundary at a point in the routine that is already yours, and it is easy to walk back if it does not fit.
change_to_try.how_to_try_it: Before you sit down after dinner, decide on a stopping point for TV or scrolling — pick a specific time, not 'when I feel like it.' When that time arrives, put the phone down or turn off the screen and move to whatever you consider creative work, even briefly. No other changes needed to start.
change_to_try.what_it_may_change: The direct effect is that a screen-free period opens before midnight that does not currently exist. That gives you a window to attempt the creative work you described wanting. Whether you use it, and whether anything about your energy or the next morning changes, is something to observe — the change creates the opening, it does not fill it.

alternatives.alternative: Moving the phone out of reach at night to address the morning scroll and the 'already behind' feeling.
alternatives.why_not_first: That is a reasonable experiment and targets a different part of the routine. I would start with the evening because you specifically named creative work there as the thing you want and are not getting — the gap between what you want and what is happening is most visible there.

signs_it_may_be_helping: You consistently reach the stopping point and screens actually go off — the screen-free window exists.
You use some of that time attempting the creative work you described wanting.
You reach the creative activity more than occasionally, not just on easy nights.
You notice some other improvement in the evening or the next day that matters to you.
signs_to_rethink_it: Screens stop but the time fills with something else you do not value — the window exists but does not go where you want.
The cutoff is consistently hard to hold in your actual evenings — it keeps slipping.
The window opens but energy is too low to use it, and that does not change after a fair trial.
The morning routine or the interrupted 4-6pm block starts to look like a more useful place to experiment.

input.routine: Wake 7am, gym 7:30-8:30, work from home 9-6 (freelance), lunch whenever, afternoon is usually most productive, evenings free but I end up working anyway. Bed around 1am. Sleep is bad.
input.goals: Better sleep, stop working evenings, make progress on a side project
input.painPoints: I have freedom but feel less productive than when I had an office job.

what_i_notice.pattern: Your workday is officially 9-6, but you describe evenings as free while also ending up working through them until around 1am. There is no clear point in the day where work stops — the boundary you said you want exists in intention but not in practice.
what_i_notice.why_it_matters: All three things you want to improve — sleep, stopping evening work, and making progress on a side project — depend on the same thing: a point where the regular work day actually ends.

change_to_try.change: Set a specific time at which you stop client work for the day — 6pm matches what you already described as the end of your workday — and treat anything after that as off-limits for it.
change_to_try.why_this_one: You already have the structure in place: a stated end time of 6pm. This change does not require building anything new, only treating a boundary you already named as real. It is reversible — if a day genuinely requires evening work, you can make that call — and it connects directly to all three things you want to improve rather than just one.
change_to_try.how_to_try_it: At 6pm, close whatever you are working on for clients and do not reopen it. If you find yourself drifting back — checking messages, picking up a task — notice it and stop. You do not need to fill the evening with anything specific; the first experiment is just whether you can hold the boundary.
change_to_try.what_it_may_change: The immediate effect is that evening hours are no longer occupied by client work. That creates a block of time that could go toward the side project you mentioned, or toward winding down before bed. Whether either of those actually happens — and whether sleep improves — is something to observe rather than assume. What you will be able to see fairly quickly is whether holding the 6pm line is feasible in your actual routine.

alternatives.alternative: Set a fixed bedtime and work backward from there.
alternatives.why_not_first: A fixed bedtime is worth trying, but if client work is still running until midnight, a bedtime target has nothing to push against. The 6pm boundary creates the space that a bedtime experiment would then operate in.

signs_it_may_be_helping: You consistently stop client work at or near 6pm most evenings.
You use some of that evening time in a way you chose — side project, rest, anything that feels like yours.
You find yourself at the side project at least occasionally, even briefly.
You notice some other improvement that matters to you — sleep, how the next morning feels, something else.
signs_to_rethink_it: You stop client work but fill the time with something else you do not value, and the evening still does not feel free.
The boundary is consistently broken by genuine client demands you cannot defer, making 6pm unrealistic.
The evening time opens up but you still cannot make contact with the side project — which would suggest the obstacle is elsewhere.
Another part of the routine — the late bedtime, or the unstructured lunch hours — starts to look like a more useful place to intervene.
